Chapter 6: Building the Qubit Hamiltonian

Centre for Quantum Software & Information, University of Technology Sydney

This is where the pipeline pays off. We take the integral tables from Chapter 3, the encoding from Chapter 5, and produce the actual qubit Hamiltonian — the object that a quantum computer will simulate.

In This Chapter¶

  • What you’ll learn: How diagonal configuration energies and off-diagonal couplings appear in a qubit Hamiltonian, how to encode fermionic terms into Pauli strings, and how to derive the 15-term H₂ result.

  • Why this matters: VQE, QPE, and Hamiltonian-simulation algorithms consume this operator. Its coefficients, signs, and Pauli weights determine both the physics and the circuit cost.

  • Prerequisites: Chapters 1–5 (integrals, notation, spin-orbitals, gates, encoding concepts).

Configuration Energies and Couplings¶

Before computing Pauli strings, separate two basis-dependent roles in the Hamiltonian. A diagonal matrix element is an energy assigned to a configuration. An off-diagonal element couples two configurations. Both belong to the same operator.

Take the two closed-shell determinants ∣g⟩=∣1100⟩|g\rangle=|1100\rangle∣g⟩=∣1100⟩ and ∣u⟩=∣0011⟩|u\rangle=|0011\rangle∣u⟩=∣0011⟩. For now write their electronic Hamiltonian block symbolically:

Hclosed=(AGGD),H_{\mathrm{closed}}= \begin{pmatrix}A&G\\G&D\end{pmatrix},Hclosed​=(AG​GD​),
(1)

where A=⟨g∣H∣g⟩A=\langle g|H|g\rangleA=⟨g∣H∣g⟩, D=⟨u∣H∣u⟩D=\langle u|H|u\rangleD=⟨u∣H∣u⟩, and G=⟨g∣H∣u⟩=⟨u∣H∣g⟩G=\langle g|H|u\rangle=\langle u|H|g\rangleG=⟨g∣H∣u⟩=⟨u∣H∣g⟩ is real in our orbital and determinant convention. We will derive their numerical values from the integrals below.

Start with a pure state¶

A normalised pure state in this block is ∣ψ⟩=α∣g⟩+β∣u⟩|\psi\rangle=\alpha|g\rangle+\beta|u\rangle∣ψ⟩=α∣g⟩+β∣u⟩ with ∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1. Expanding its expectation value rather than naming it gives

Eψ=(α∗⟨g∣+β∗⟨u∣)H(α∣g⟩+β∣u⟩)=∣α∣2A+∣β∣2D+α∗βG+β∗αG=∣α∣2A+∣β∣2D+2G Re⁡(α∗β).\begin{aligned} E_\psi &=(\alpha^*\langle g|+\beta^*\langle u|) H(\alpha|g\rangle+\beta|u\rangle)\\ &=|\alpha|^2A+|\beta|^2D +\alpha^*\beta G+\beta^*\alpha G\\ &=|\alpha|^2A+|\beta|^2D+2G\,\operatorname{Re}(\alpha^*\beta). \end{aligned}Eψ​​=(α∗⟨g∣+β∗⟨u∣)H(α∣g⟩+β∣u⟩)=∣α∣2A+∣β∣2D+α∗βG+β∗αG=∣α∣2A+∣β∣2D+2GRe(α∗β).​
(2)

The first two terms use configuration energies. The last term depends on a relative phase and uses the configuration coupling. For equal real amplitudes, changing β\betaβ from +1/2+1/\sqrt2+1/2​ to −1/2-1/\sqrt2−1/2​ changes the energy from (A+D)/2+G(A+D)/2+G(A+D)/2+G to (A+D)/2−G(A+D)/2-G(A+D)/2−G, without changing either configuration’s probability.

Compare with a mixture having the same populations¶

Suppose instead we toss a classical coin and prepare ∣g⟩|g\rangle∣g⟩ with probability ppp, otherwise ∣u⟩|u\rangle∣u⟩. There is no fixed relative phase between those separately prepared states. Averaging their energies gives

Emix=pA+(1−p)D.E_{\mathrm{mix}}=pA+(1-p)D.Emix​=pA+(1−p)D.
(3)

Choosing p=∣α∣2p=|\alpha|^2p=∣α∣2 matches the pure state’s computational-basis probabilities but loses its cross term. This is the same superposition-versus-mixture distinction as the Bell example in Chapter 4, now with an energy consequence.

Density matrices abbreviate both calculations¶

The outer product ∣v⟩⟨w∣|v\rangle\langle w|∣v⟩⟨w∣ is an operator: it takes an overlap with ∣w⟩|w\rangle∣w⟩ and returns a multiple of ∣v⟩|v\rangle∣v⟩. For a pure state define its density matrix ρψ=∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣\rho_\psi=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|ρψ​=∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣. For a statistical mixture of states ∣ψk⟩|\psi_k\rangle∣ψk​⟩ prepared with probabilities pkp_kpk​, define ρ=∑kpk∣ψk⟩⟨ψk∣\rho=\sum_k p_k|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|ρ=∑k​pk​∣ψk​⟩⟨ψk​∣. These matrices are Hermitian and positive semidefinite (their eigenvalues are nonnegative). Their diagonal entries sum to one. Here the two examples are

ρψ=(∣α∣2αβ∗βα∗∣β∣2),ρmix=(p001−p).\rho_\psi=\begin{pmatrix} |\alpha|^2&\alpha\beta^*\\ \beta\alpha^*&|\beta|^2 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{mix}}=\begin{pmatrix}p&0\\0&1-p\end{pmatrix}.ρψ​=(∣α∣2βα∗​αβ∗∣β∣2​),ρmix​=(p0​01−p​).
(4)

The trace, Tr⁡(B)=∑iBii\operatorname{Tr}(B)=\sum_iB_{ii}Tr(B)=∑i​Bii​, is the sum of a matrix’s diagonal entries. Multiplying first, then taking that sum, recovers both expectation formulae:

⟨H⟩=Tr⁡(ρH)=∑iρiiHii+∑i≠jρijHji.\langle H\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H) =\sum_i\rho_{ii}H_{ii}+\sum_{i\ne j}\rho_{ij}H_{ji}.⟨H⟩=Tr(ρH)=i∑​ρii​Hii​+i=j∑​ρij​Hji​.
(5)

Off-diagonal density entries are called coherences in the chosen basis. A mixed state need not be diagonal in every basis; our coin preparation is diagonal specifically in the determinant basis. Likewise an energy eigenstate has no off-diagonal entries in its own eigenbasis. “Diagonal” is not an absolute label for classical physics.

Off-diagonal Hamiltonian elements can lower the optimised energy by mixing determinants. That does not make correlation energy equal to the expectation of just those elements: the optimal populations change too. Correlation energy compares the optimised correlated and Hartree–Fock expectations of the full Hamiltonian.

A Hamiltonian diagonal in the occupation basis has computational-basis eigenstates, so coherence cannot lower its minimum eigenvalue. Degeneracy may also permit coherent ground states, but it gives no energetic advantage over a basis-state ground state. In JW, terms containing XXX or YYY connect occupation configurations. Evolution cost depends on weight, however: a weight-two ZZZZZZ rotation also uses entangling gates, while a weight-one XXX rotation does not. Measuring a string is a separate task from evolving under it.

Encoding changes the Pauli representation of both diagonal and off-diagonal fermionic operators. The practical question is not which part is “classical” or “quantum” in an absolute sense, but how accurately and cheaply the chosen representation implements the full operator.

What We Have and What We’ll Do¶

Chapters 1–4 gave us everything we need:

  • The chemistry (Chapter 1): H₂ in STO-3G, 4 spin-orbitals, the second-quantized Hamiltonian.

  • The notation (Chapter 2): physicist’s convention, the conversion rule, the traps to avoid.

  • The numbers (Chapter 3): complete spin-orbital integral tables and a coefficient factory in F#.

  • The quantum computer (Chapter 4): qubits, gates, CNOT cost, and the 2(w−1)2(w-1)2(w−1) formula.

  • The encoding (Chapter 5): Jordan–Wigner’s Z-chain mechanism for translating fermionic operators to Pauli strings.

The procedure is systematic, but every new input still needs an integral- convention check, a direct matrix reference where feasible, and a validated encoding implementation.

The Recipe¶

FockMap multiplies and collects symbolic Pauli operators rather than constructing dense matrices. Their signs and phases follow a discrete algebra; their molecular coefficients remain finite-precision numbers. We will do the multiplication and collection explicitly enough to recover every entry of the final table.

One-body terms: number operators¶

The non-zero one-body integrals for H₂ are all diagonal (Chapter 3): h00=h11=−1.2533097866h_{00} = h_{11} = -1.2533097866h00​=h11​=−1.2533097866 Ha and h22=h33=−0.4750688488h_{22} = h_{33} = -0.4750688488h22​=h33​=−0.4750688488 Ha. Under Jordan–Wigner, the number operator simplifies — the Z-chains cancel:

n^j=aj†aj=12(I−Zj)\hat{n}_j = a_j^\dagger a_j = \frac{1}{2}(I - Z_j)n^j​=aj†​aj​=21​(I−Zj​)
(6)

Weight 1, regardless of system size. The one-body Hamiltonian produces five diagonal terms:

IIIIIIIIIIII-1.7283786354Sum of diagonal one-body integrals, halved
ZIIIZIIIZIII+0.6266548933−h00/2-h_{00}/2−h00​/2 (energy of σg,α\sigma_g, \alphaσg​,α)
IZIIIZIIIZII+0.6266548933−h11/2-h_{11}/2−h11​/2 (energy of σg,β\sigma_g, \betaσg​,β)
IIZIIIZIIIZI+0.2375344244−h22/2-h_{22}/2−h22​/2 (energy of σu,α\sigma_u, \alphaσu​,α)
IIIZIIIZIIIZ+0.2375344244−h33/2-h_{33}/2−h33​/2 (energy of σu,β\sigma_u, \betaσu​,β)

All I and Z. By itself, this operator cannot mix occupation configurations; its eigenvalues are read directly from computational-basis states.

After the symmetry-related index permutations are combined, the Coulomb repulsion between opposite-spin electrons in σg\sigma_gσg​ contributes 0.6747559268 a0†a1†a1a00.6747559268\,a_0^\dagger a_1^\dagger a_1a_00.6747559268a0†​a1†​a1​a0​.

a0†a1†a1a0=14(IIII−ZIII−IZII+ZZII)a_0^\dagger a_1^\dagger a_1 a_0 = \frac{1}{4}(IIII - ZIII - IZII + ZZII)a0†​a1†​a1​a0​=41​(IIII−ZIII−IZII+ZZII)

Scaled by the integral, this gives four diagonal Pauli contributions.

Collect all diagonal contributions¶

Use short names for the four spatial integral values:

Jg=[00∣00]=0.6747559268,Ju=[11∣11]=0.6976515045,J=[00∣11]=0.6637114014,g=[01∣01]=0.1812104620,\begin{aligned} J_g&=[00|00]=0.6747559268, & J_u&=[11|11]=0.6976515045,\\ J&=[00|11]=0.6637114014, & g&=[01|01]=0.1812104620 , \end{aligned}Jg​J​=[00∣00]=0.6747559268,=[00∣11]=0.6637114014,​Ju​g​=[11∣11]=0.6976515045,=[01∣01]=0.1812104620,​

all in hartree. Here JJJ is a Coulomb integral between the two different MOs and ggg also supplies same-spin exchange. For opposite spins the exchange spin overlap vanishes; for same spins it survives. Combining the raw integral permutations as in Chapter 2 yields six occupied-pair coefficients:

Hdiag=hg(n^0+n^1)+hu(n^2+n^3)+Jgn^0n^1+Jun^2n^3+J(n^0n^3+n^1n^2)+(J−g)(n^0n^2+n^1n^3).\begin{aligned} H_{\mathrm{diag}}={}&h_g(\hat n_0+\hat n_1) +h_u(\hat n_2+\hat n_3) +J_g\hat n_0\hat n_1+J_u\hat n_2\hat n_3\\ &+J(\hat n_0\hat n_3+\hat n_1\hat n_2) +(J-g)(\hat n_0\hat n_2+\hat n_1\hat n_3). \end{aligned}Hdiag​=​hg​(n^0​+n^1​)+hu​(n^2​+n^3​)+Jg​n^0​n^1​+Ju​n^2​n^3​+J(n^0​n^3​+n^1​n^2​)+(J−g)(n^0​n^2​+n^1​n^3​).​

Every pair contributes Vpq(I−Zp−Zq+ZpZq)/4V_{pq}(I-Z_p-Z_q+Z_pZ_q)/4Vpq​(I−Zp​−Zq​+Zp​Zq​)/4. This gives a compact coefficient ledger:

cI=hg+hu+Jg+Ju+4J−2g4,cZ0=cZ1=−hg2−Jg+2J−g4,cZ2=cZ3=−hu2−Ju+2J−g4,cZ0Z1=Jg/4,cZ2Z3=Ju/4,cZ0Z3=cZ1Z2=J/4,cZ0Z2=cZ1Z3=(J−g)/4.\begin{aligned} c_I&=h_g+h_u+\frac{J_g+J_u+4J-2g}{4},\\ c_{Z_0}=c_{Z_1} &=-\frac{h_g}{2}-\frac{J_g+2J-g}{4},\\ c_{Z_2}=c_{Z_3} &=-\frac{h_u}{2}-\frac{J_u+2J-g}{4},\\ c_{Z_0Z_1}&=J_g/4,\qquad c_{Z_2Z_3}=J_u/4,\\ c_{Z_0Z_3}=c_{Z_1Z_2}&=J/4,\qquad c_{Z_0Z_2}=c_{Z_1Z_3}=(J-g)/4. \end{aligned}cI​cZ0​​=cZ1​​cZ2​​=cZ3​​cZ0​Z1​​cZ0​Z3​​=cZ1​Z2​​​=hg​+hu​+4Jg​+Ju​+4J−2g​,=−2hg​​−4Jg​+2J−g​,=−2hu​​−4Ju​+2J−g​,=Jg​/4,cZ2​Z3​​=Ju​/4,=J/4,cZ0​Z2​​=cZ1​Z3​​=(J−g)/4.​
(10)

For example, (J−g)/4=0.1206252348(J-g)/4=0.1206252348(J−g)/4=0.1206252348 Ha to the precision displayed in the final table. The identity coefficient is -0.8121706072 Ha. It includes the constants introduced when rewriting number operators, but not nuclear repulsion. We now have all eleven diagonal strings: identity, four single ZZZs, and six ZZZZZZs.

The four coupling monomials¶

Number products cannot connect different configurations. The remaining nonzero, collected quartic terms transfer an opposite-spin pair or exchange the occupied spin-orbitals. Set

Af=a0†a1†a3a2,Cf=a0†a3†a2a1.A_f=a_0^\dagger a_1^\dagger a_3a_2,\qquad C_f=a_0^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_2a_1.Af​=a0†​a1†​a3​a2​,Cf​=a0†​a3†​a2​a1​.
(11)

The subscript distinguishes these fermionic monomials from the diagonal block entry AAA. Their adjoints reverse the whole operator product:

Af†=a2†a3†a1a0,Cf†=a1†a2†a3a0.A_f^\dagger=a_2^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_1a_0,\qquad C_f^\dagger=a_1^\dagger a_2^\dagger a_3a_0.Af†​=a2†​a3†​a1​a0​,Cf†​=a1†​a2†​a3​a0​.
(12)

The off-diagonal contribution is

Hcouple=g(a0†a1†a3a2+a2†a3†a1a0−a0†a3†a2a1−a1†a2†a3a0).\begin{aligned} H_{\mathrm{couple}}=g(&a_0^\dagger a_1^\dagger a_3a_2 +a_2^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_1a_0\\ &-a_0^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_2a_1 -a_1^\dagger a_2^\dagger a_3a_0). \end{aligned}Hcouple​=g(​a0†​a1†​a3​a2​+a2†​a3†​a1​a0​−a0†​a3†​a2​a1​−a1†​a2†​a3​a0​).​
(13)

The first line transfers an opposite-spin pair between the bonding and antibonding orbitals; the second line contains the associated spin-exchange terms. Their relative sign is already present before encoding. In the restricted antisymmetrised notation, for example,

⟨01∥23⟩=g−0=g,⟨03∥12⟩=0−g=−g.\langle01\Vert23\rangle=g-0=g,\qquad \langle03\Vert12\rangle=0-g=-g.⟨01∥23⟩=g−0=g,⟨03∥12⟩=0−g=−g.
(14)

The zero in each subtraction comes from the spin deltas of Chapter 3. The second coefficient multiplies a0†a3†a2a1=Cfa_0^\dagger a_3^\dagger a_2a_1=C_fa0†​a3†​a2​a1​=Cf​. The reverse transfers have the same real coefficients. Thus Hcouple=g(Af+Af†−Cf−Cf†)H_{\mathrm{couple}}=g(A_f+A_f^\dagger-C_f-C_f^\dagger)Hcouple​=g(Af​+Af†​−Cf​−Cf†​).

Expand one monomial completely¶

Substitute the four JW ladders into AfA_fAf​. Keeping their written order,

Af=116(X0−iY0)Z0(X1−iY1)Z0Z1Z2(X3+iY3)Z0Z1(X2+iY2).A_f=\frac1{16}(X_0-iY_0) Z_0(X_1-iY_1) Z_0Z_1Z_2(X_3+iY_3) Z_0Z_1(X_2+iY_2).Af​=161​(X0​−iY0​)Z0​(X1​−iY1​)Z0​Z1​Z2​(X3​+iY3​)Z0​Z1​(X2​+iY2​).
(15)

Operators on different qubits can be gathered without a sign. At qubit 0, (X−iY)Z=X−iY(X-iY)Z=X-iY(X−iY)Z=X−iY and the remaining two ZZZs cancel. At qubit 1, the two later ZZZs cancel. At qubit 2, Z(X+iY)=X+iYZ(X+iY)=X+iYZ(X+iY)=X+iY. We obtain

Af=116(X0−iY0)(X1−iY1)(X2+iY2)(X3+iY3).A_f=\frac1{16} (X_0-iY_0)(X_1-iY_1)(X_2+iY_2)(X_3+iY_3).Af​=161​(X0​−iY0​)(X1​−iY1​)(X2​+iY2​)(X3​+iY3​).
(16)

Choose XXX or YYY at each of four positions: there are sixteen terms. If the chosen YYY positions are a set SSS, the coefficient is (−i)∣S∩{0,1}∣i∣S∩{2,3}∣/16(-i)^{|S\cap\{0,1\}|}i^{|S\cap\{2,3\}|}/16(−i)∣S∩{0,1}∣i∣S∩{2,3}∣/16. For XXYY this is i2/16=−1/16i^2/16=-1/16i2/16=−1/16. For XYYX it is (−i)i/16=+1/16(-i)i/16=+1/16(−i)i/16=+1/16. For XXXY it is i/16i/16i/16: a single monomial is not Hermitian.

The other transfer has the analogous product

Cf=116(X0−iY0)(X1+iY1)(X2+iY2)(X3−iY3).C_f=\frac1{16} (X_0-iY_0)(X_1+iY_1)(X_2+iY_2)(X_3-iY_3).Cf​=161​(X0​−iY0​)(X1​+iY1​)(X2​+iY2​)(X3​−iY3​).

Check a labelled transition before diagonalising¶

Each of the four strings takes ∣0011⟩|0011\rangle∣0011⟩ to ∣1100⟩|1100\rangle∣1100⟩, but with different phases:

The matrix element is therefore +g+g+g, as the original pair transfer requires. A table of coefficients has become one concrete operator action. In the occupation-integer matrix this is row 3, column 12, not row 12 because the label happens to start with 11.

Reading the Hamiltonian: Where the Energy Lowering Comes From¶

Now we read this table through the density matrix lens.

Eleven terms contain only I and Z. Together they assign an energy to each occupation configuration. Four weight-four terms couple the closed-shell determinants ∣1100⟩|1100\rangle∣1100⟩ and ∣0011⟩|0011\rangle∣0011⟩, and also the open-shell opposite-spin determinants ∣1001⟩|1001\rangle∣1001⟩ and ∣0110⟩|0110\rangle∣0110⟩. For this integral tensor, these are separate two-dimensional blocks.

The closed-shell block¶

In ∣1100⟩|1100\rangle∣1100⟩ only n^0,n^1\hat n_0,\hat n_1n^0​,n^1​ are nonzero, so A=2hg+JgA=2h_g+J_gA=2hg​+Jg​. In ∣0011⟩|0011\rangle∣0011⟩, D=2hu+JuD=2h_u+J_uD=2hu​+Ju​. The off-diagonal calculation above supplies G=gG=gG=g, giving

Hclosed≈(−1.8318636465+0.1812104620+0.1812104620−0.2524861931) Ha.H_{\mathrm{closed}}\approx \begin{pmatrix} -1.8318636465&+0.1812104620\\ +0.1812104620&-0.2524861931 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{Ha}.Hclosed​≈(−1.8318636465+0.1812104620​+0.1812104620−0.2524861931​) Ha.
(19)

The displayed inputs are rounded; the following reference energies use the canonical full-precision data. For a real symmetric block the characteristic equation is

det⁡(Hclosed−EI)=(A−E)(D−E)−g2=0,\det(H_{\mathrm{closed}}-EI)=(A-E)(D-E)-g^2=0,det(Hclosed​−EI)=(A−E)(D−E)−g2=0,
(20)

so

E±=A+D2±(D−A2)2+g2.E_\pm=\frac{A+D}{2} \pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{D-A}{2}\right)^2+g^2}.E±​=2A+D​±(2D−A​)2+g2​.
(21)

This yields E−=−1.8523881736E_-=-1.8523881736E−​=−1.8523881736 Ha and E+=−0.2319616660E_+=-0.2319616660E+​=−0.2319616660 Ha. Since the square root exceeds (D−A)/2(D-A)/2(D−A)/2 when g≠0g\ne0g=0, the lower eigenvalue is below AAA. That is the energy benefit of mixing, obtained without a variational optimiser or a quantum device.

Solve (A−E−)α+gβ=0(A-E_-)\alpha+g\beta=0(A−E−​)α+gβ=0 to recover the state:

βα=E−−Ag<0,∣ψ−⟩≈0.99364675 ∣1100⟩−0.11254389 ∣0011⟩.\frac{\beta}{\alpha}=\frac{E_--A}{g}<0,\qquad |\psi_-\rangle\approx 0.99364675\,|1100\rangle-0.11254389\,|0011\rangle.αβ​=gE−​−A​<0,∣ψ−​⟩≈0.99364675∣1100⟩−0.11254389∣0011⟩.
(22)

The negative relative sign is selected by the positive coupling. Its squared RHF overlap is approximately 0.98733387, while the antibonding-pair probability is 0.01266613. These probabilities sum to one; neither is itself an energy.

The two same-spin determinants have energy hg+hu+J−g=−1.2458776961h_g+h_u+J-g =-1.2458776961hg​+hu​+J−g=−1.2458776961 Ha. The opposite-spin open-shell block has diagonal hg+hu+Jh_g+h_u+Jhg​+hu​+J and off-diagonal −g-g−g, with eigenvalues -1.2458776961 and -0.8834567721 Ha. This accounts for all six two-electron states and confirms that E−E_-E−​ is the two-electron ground energy, not merely the lower eigenvalue of an arbitrarily selected block.

Figure 6.1. The closed-shell H₂ block in the chosen determinant phase convention. Diagonal entries are configuration energies; the connecting entry is a matrix element, not an extra energy added once to each state. All values are electronic, for H₂/STO-3G at 0.74 Å.

Reconcile the pure-state and mixture energies¶

Deleting the four coupling strings (rows 8–11 in the Pauli table) makes ∣1100⟩|1100\rangle∣1100⟩ the lowest two-electron determinant. Its electronic energy is -1.8318636465 Ha; adding Vnn=0.7151043391V_{nn}=0.7151043391Vnn​=0.7151043391 Ha gives -1.1167593074 Ha. This equals RHF because the chosen MOs are the RHF orbitals and the reference determinant is the lowest diagonal configuration for this example. It is not a general algorithm for doing HF with arbitrary fixed orbitals.

Restoring the coupling gives total FCI energy −1.8523881736+0.7151043391=−1.1372838345-1.8523881736+0.7151043391=-1.1372838345−1.8523881736+0.7151043391=−1.1372838345 Ha.

The decomposition makes the earlier warning concrete. In the exact ground state, changed determinant populations raise the diagonal expectation by about 0.0200046 Ha relative to the HF determinant, while the off-diagonal expectation contributes about -0.0405291 Ha. Their sum is the net correlation energy, -0.0205245 Ha (about -12.88 kcal/mol). The correlation energy is therefore enabled by the coupling but does not “live entirely” in four expectation values.

Using the amplitudes just computed, the two contributions can be recovered separately:

Ediag−A=∣β∣2(D−A)≈+0.0200045946 Ha,Ecouple=2gαβ≈−0.0405291217 Ha,E−−A≈−0.0205245271 Ha.\begin{aligned} E_{\mathrm{diag}}-A&=|\beta|^2(D-A) \approx+0.0200045946\ \text{Ha},\\ E_{\mathrm{couple}}&=2g\alpha\beta \approx-0.0405291217\ \text{Ha},\\ E_--A&\approx-0.0205245271\ \text{Ha}. \end{aligned}Ediag​−AEcouple​E−​−A​=∣β∣2(D−A)≈+0.0200045946 Ha,=2gαβ≈−0.0405291217 Ha,≈−0.0205245271 Ha.​
(23)

A mixture with these same determinant populations has energy Ediag≈−1.8118590519E_{\mathrm{diag}}\approx-1.8118590519Ediag​≈−1.8118590519 Ha, which is above RHF. Mixing in the expensive antibonding determinant only pays because the coherent cross term lowers the energy by more than that population change costs. Saying “the state has 1.27% of the excited determinant” does not explain the energy until its relative phase and coupling are also specified.

Constructing with FockMap¶

Run dotnet fsi code/ch06-building-hamiltonian.fsx from the repository root for the complete companion. The following construction excerpt loads the Chapter 3 raw factory, assembles the JW Hamiltonian, and prints the collected nonzero terms. The companion’s assertions and comparison reporting are separate from this short listing:

#load "code/ch03-spin-orbitals.fsx"

open System.Numerics
open Encodings
open Encodings.Hamiltonian

let h2RawPhysicistFactory =
    ``Ch03-spin-orbitals``.h2RawPhysicistFactory

let hamiltonian =
    computeHamiltonian h2RawPhysicistFactory 4u

let terms =
    hamiltonian.DistributeCoefficient.SummandTerms
    |> Array.filter (fun t -> Complex.Abs t.Coefficient > 1e-12)
    |> Array.sortBy (fun t -> t.Signature)

for t in terms do
    printfn "%+.4f  %s" t.Coefficient.Real t.Signature

Output:

-0.8122  IIII
-0.2234  IIIZ
-0.2234  IIZI
+0.1744  IIZZ
+0.1714  IZII
+0.1206  IZIZ
+0.1659  IZZI
-0.0453  XXYY
+0.0453  XYYX
+0.0453  YXXY
-0.0453  YYXX
+0.1714  ZIII
+0.1659  ZIIZ
+0.1206  ZIZI
+0.1687  ZZII

computeHamiltonian applies the raw two-body half and the asara_s a_ras​ar​ order; the factory has not already done so. DistributeCoefficient.SummandTerms exposes individual weighted strings for inspection. The reporting filter removes numerically tiny coefficients, not missing physical interactions. Inspecting real parts for printing is appropriate for this Hermitian result; it is not permission to discard imaginary discrepancies in a matrix check.

The canonical result has 15 assembled nonzero terms. Equal term counts or two sentinel coefficients alone would not establish the complete operator. Chapter 9 compares full coefficients, labelled actions, matrices and spectra against independent construction. The coefficient 1-norm λcoeff=∑k∣ck∣=2.6992778241\lambda_{\mathrm{coeff}}=\sum_k|c_k|=2.6992778241λcoeff​=∑k​∣ck​∣=2.6992778241 Ha includes the identity term; it is not the commutator quantity used in Chapter 15.

There is also a useful arithmetic check on the displayed table. Its total Pauli weight is

0+4(1)+6(2)+4(4)=32.0+4(1)+6(2)+4(4)=32.0+4(1)+6(2)+4(4)=32.
(24)

Under Chapter 4’s standard logical staircase, evolving once under each nonidentity term requires

4(0)+6(2)+4(6)=36 CNOTs.4(0)+6(2)+4(6)=36\ \text{CNOTs}.4(0)+6(2)+4(6)=36 CNOTs.
(25)

There are 14 nonidentity rotations, not 15: the identity term contributes only a global phase to ordinary uncontrolled evolution. Controlled evolution needs that phase accounted for separately, as later chapters explain. These are counts for one untapered first-order logical product, not a complete energy-estimation algorithm or an experimental resource estimate.

We now have an inspectable JW reference. Chapter 7 introduces the other encoders and shows how to pass an encoder to computeHamiltonianWith; Chapter 9 checks the results with the corresponding state/basis map. An encoding comparison is the next lesson, not an unexplained extra argument in this one.

Key Takeaways¶

  • A diagonal density matrix represents a classical mixture in the chosen basis; off-diagonal entries retain coherence between configurations.

  • Off-diagonal Hamiltonian terms couple configurations, but correlation energy is the change in the optimised expectation of the full Hamiltonian.

  • The direct H₂ JW Hamiltonian has 11 diagonal terms and 4 configuration-coupling terms.

  • Encoding changes supports and state representation. The collected weights determine a specified logical staircase count; complete simulation cost needs additional algorithm and compilation choices.

Common Mistakes¶

  1. Remember to add VnnV_{nn}Vnn​ when computing total energy. The 15-term Hamiltonian above is the purely electronic Hamiltonian. Its eigenvalues are electronic energies EelE_\text{el}Eel​. To get the total molecular energy, add the nuclear repulsion: Etotal=Eel+VnnE_\text{total} = E_\text{el} + V_{nn}Etotal​=Eel​+Vnn​. (For H₂, Vnn=0.7151V_{nn} = 0.7151Vnn​=0.7151 Ha.)

  2. Wrong operator ordering. Writing arasa_r a_sar​as​ instead of asara_s a_ras​ar​ negates every surviving quartic monomial, including pair energies. Taking an adjoint reverses the entire product, not just the annihilators.

  3. Not combining like terms. The 32 two-body integrals produce many duplicate Pauli signatures that must be summed.

Exercises¶

  1. Number operator by hand. Verify that a2†a2=12(I−Z2)a_2^\dagger a_2 = \frac{1}{2}(I - Z_2)a2†​a2​=21​(I−Z2​) by expanding the JW-encoded operators.

  2. Coupling-term sign. Starting from the four-monomial expression above, explain why XXYYXXYYXXYY has coefficient -0.0453026155 and XYYXXYYXXYYX has +0.0453026155.

  3. Diagonal-only energy. Delete coupling terms 8–11, retaining all eleven I/Z strings. Evaluate the six two-electron configurations and identify the minimum electronic energy. Add VnnV_{nn}Vnn​ to obtain the total RHF energy. Why is this deletion different from omitting the cross-spin integrals in Chapter 3?

  4. Closed-shell eigenstate. Use AAA, DDD and ggg from the block to solve its characteristic equation and normalise (1,(E−−A)/g)(1,(E_--A)/g)(1,(E−​−A)/g). Report electronic energy, total energy and RHF overlap separately.

  5. Same populations, different energy. Construct the pure-state and mixture density matrices using the ground-state amplitudes. Recover their energies by direct matrix multiplication and trace. Explain why the mixture’s energy is above RHF even though the coherent state’s is below it.

  6. One cancellation, one survivor. In the sixteen-row expansion, derive the four contributions to XYXY and XYYX without reading their final sums. Why does one signature disappear while the other has coefficient +g/4+g/4+g/4?

  7. Resource arithmetic. Recover total weight 32 and logical CNOT count 36 from the fifteen-term table. Explain why there are fourteen nonidentity rotations and why those thirty-six CNOTs are not required merely to measure all the Pauli expectations.
